newsitem.title: GERMANY: Two-yr M3 goal base for policy coordination - Buba.
newsitem.headline: Two-yr M3 goal base for policy coordination - Buba.

text.p: The Bundesbank's decision in December last year to set a two-year orientation path for German money supply growth means a reference point is set for policy coordination up until 1999, the Bundesbank said.

In its January monthly report, published on Thursday, the German central bank argued forcefully for the new European bank to adopt some form of money supply target strategy to guide its monetary policy, the practice adopted by the Bundesbank itself.
It said its decision to give this year's German M3 target a two-year orientation meant the new bank could tack on its policy seamlessly to the Bundesbank's stability course.
It would also allow European central banks to coordinate their policies more smoothly over the next two years, before the European Central Bank (ECB) assumes policy control in 1997.
"Additionally, the statement of a two-year intention could serve as a sort of reference size for the coordination of monetary policy which may be necessary," the report said.

The Bundesbank in December diverted slightly from its usual policy of setting a one-year M3 goal by adding a second general comment on the way in which it expected its main monetary policy indicator to develop in 1998.
It set an expansion corridor of 3-1/2 to 6-1/2 percent for 1997, based on a central growth rate of five percent, and said it also expected M3 to grow by five percent on average in 1998.

The two-year target, which bridges the gap between the decision in early 1998 on which countries qualify to join the single currency and the establishment of the ECB, was set partly with a view to calming financial markets in that time.

Noting that this also paved the way for the future ECB to adopt a monetary policy targeting strategy -- on which no decision has yet been made -- the Bundesbank strongly recommended this course of action to the future bank.
"Orientation by means of the money supply -- in whatever detailed form it may take -- should, in the Bundesbank's view, be adopted within the concept of the ECB," the report said.
The policy strategy to be adopted by the ECB will not be decided until its officials are appointed some time in 1998.

But its forerunner, the European Monetary Institute, said last week in a report that either money supply or inflation targeting could be possible strategies for it to adopt, ruling out the use of exchange rate, interest rate or income targets.

The Bundesbank said that use of a money supply orientation would be very useful, given that the ECB will initially be acting in an uncertain environment as regards monetary relationships and the transmission of monetary impulses within the euro area, and also be working to build up credibility.
"Without a convincing precommitment to stability policies it will not be able to survive in this situation," it said.

"A pragmatic money supply strategy, tailored to the special requirements of this currency area, would therefore appear important as a way to carry the concept through the opening phase, which will be difficult anyway," it added.
The Bundesbank, guardian of Europe's anchor currency, the mark, currently de facto sets interest rates throughout Europe.
The establishment of a ECB whose policy has similar degree of credibility to that of the inflation-conscious Bundesbank is seen as crucial if the euro is to be a stable, successful currency.
